content:
Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator, in which Epic accuses Apple of adopting a restrictive interpretation of its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust agreement reached in Brazil. Here are the details.

A little background

Two months ago, Apple announced it would now allow developers to distribute apps in Brazil through alternative app marketplaces.

The change was part of a settlement deal with Brazil that ended a years-long antitrust investigation, which was triggered by a complaint from Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "core technology fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. More information on the structure can be found here.

Epic questions Apple's implementation

According to Brazilian newspaper O Globo (via MacMagazine) today, Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, accusing Apple of imposing "structural, technical and access barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution channels.

Epic pointed out that while Brazil's new terms apply only to iOS apps, the agreement Apple reached with CADE "clearly covers iPadOS" as well.

The company is also reportedly challenging so-called "scare screens" that discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store, and is criticising the current installation process, which it says requires nine steps, compared to six steps in Apple's current European implementation.

O Globo reported that Epic added that Apple's initial European installation process required 15 steps, but after being forced to reduce it to six, the "download abandonment rate fell from 65% to 25%".

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is needed to calculate fees," and said this allows the company to "monitor competitors' business models".

O Globo said CADE has given Apple until Monday to respond. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
